title: Sex monster's desperate last act after Labor guru's vile guilt exposed
text:
By STEPHEN GIBBS, SENIOR NEWS REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  18:31 AEST, 27 August 2026   |  Updated:  01:43 AEST, 28 August 2026

14

View  comments

A former senior government adviser who was secretly tried for child sex crimes while his identity was suppressed due to a clerical error swallowed a bottle of painkillers after he was found guilty.

Daily Mail can reveal the final desperate act of Craig Munnings when he realised his seven years of hiding behind a bungled court order was over and he would finally be exposed as a paedophile.

Munnings served as an adviser to NSW Labor ministers Ian Macdonald, John Aquilina, Di Beamer and Harry Woods during a 12-year political career in and around Macquarie Street.

The 61-year-old married father-of-two, from Woy Woy on the Central Coast, is also an ordained Anglican minister who once ran unsuccessfully as a Labor local government candidate.

Munnings was charged with child sex crimes in February 2019 and a non-publication order was mistakenly made over his name when he faced court for the first time the following month.

He has always denied sexually assaulting two girls - one of whom was just 10 when his abuse began - in the mid-1980s and early 1990s.

Munnings had been set to face a jury as early as 2020, and spent seven years on bail as the proceedings were continually pushed back and several trials were aborted.

While on bail, he continued operating his consultancy businesses and even travelled overseas before being found guilty of 14 child sex offences at Gosford District Court on August 7.

Former senior government adviser Craig Munnings, whose name was suppressed due to a clerical error while he faced trial for child sex crimes, swallowed a bottle of pills when the jury returned guilty verdicts. Munnings is pictured

Munnings spent seven years on bail before he was found guilty of 14 child sex offences at Gosford District Court (above) earlier this month

Trial dates had been set nine times between August 2020 and July 2026. A jury in one of three aborted trials was discharged after the Crown raised concerns Munnings's opening address was prejudicial.

Munnings has variously claimed to have prostate cancer, to have had a heart attack and to require heart surgery. He also unsuccessfully applied for Legal Aid and has not had a lawyer since 2022.

Another trial began on July 6 but was aborted the next day when two of 14 jurors could not continue. A fresh jury was empanelled on July 8 and the trial ran for a month.

Munnings represented himself, pleading not guilty to nine counts of sexual assault, four of aggravated indecent assault of a victim under 16, and one of carnal knowledge of a girl aged between 10 and 16.

The victims' evidence and their cross-examination by a barrister acting on Munnings's behalf had been recorded for his first scheduled trial in 2020 and was tendered again.

On August 7, the jury returned after four hours and 46 minutes of deliberations and found Munnings guilty of all 14 offences.

As the jury foreman began reading out the panel's findings, a female court officer saw that Munnings, who was sitting at the bar table, had upended a bottle of pills into his mouth.

According to a witness who was watching the proceedings via an audio-visual link, the court officer said words to the effect of, 'Stop! Don't take those!'

Munnings (above) served as an adviser to NSW Labor ministers Ian Macdonald, John Aquilina, Di Beamer and Harry Woods during a 12-year political career

The court officer then rushed to the bar table and asked Munnings, 'What was that?' as Judge Gordon Lerve turned from the jury and looked at the offender.

When Munnings said, 'It's just my prescription medication, my painkillers', the court officer replied, 'But you've taken the whole bottle.'

Munnings, who claimed to have swallowed only three tablets, told Judge Lerve, 'My feet are giving me pain so I needed to take these pills.'

The jury foreman resumed delivering the guilty verdicts but when Judge Lerve spoke to Munnings he was slurring his words, according to the witness.

After proposals to remove the suppression order and revoke Munnings's bail were raised, Judge Lerve took an early lunch adjournment.

When the court reassembled, a sheriff told Judge Lerve that during the break Munnings had been seen with an empty unmarked pill bottle, falling asleep in his chair.

Fearing Munnings had overdosed on the painkillers, authorities contacted the NSW Poisons Information Centre and he was taken by ambulance to hospital.

Munnings was transferred to Parklea Correctional Centre in Sydney's north-west upon his release later that day and remains there ahead of being sentenced.

Munnings was taken by ambulance to hospital after swallowing painkillers at Gosford District Court after being found guilty of child sex offences. Stock image

Observers of the Munnings case had been perplexed - then angered - when there was almost no media coverage as his prosecution dragged on through the courts for years.

Daily Mail understands that when it emerged during the final trial that Munnings had mistakenly been protected by a non-publication order, a decision was made to leave it in place until the hearing had finished.

The case had been delayed so many times - including once when Munnings said his wife had been diagnosed with cancer - that any further interruption was considered too risky.

The non-publication order should have covered only the names of the two sexual assault victims or anything which might tend to identify them.

But when entered into Justicelink, the digital electronic case management system used across NSW courts, the order had erroneously included Munnings.

'The name of the defendant was temporarily suppressed in a clerical error that has now been rectified,' a spokesman for NSW Local Court said.

Munnings first came to police attention when Brisbane Water detectives launched an investigation into allegations of child sexual abuse at Woy Woy in September 2016.

He was a 19-year-old youth leader when he started abusing his first victim and an ordained pastor by the time he began assaulting a 15-year-old girl who came forward in 2020.

Munnings's company Crakyl Pty Ltd, which he owns with his wife, is still listed on The Lobbyists Register for the NSW parliament. Munnings is pictured

Munnings was not named in the initial meagre media coverage of his arrest, when he was referred to as a 54-year-old church volunteer and Labor Party member.

The party suspended his membership the day of his first court appearance, with a spokesman saying: 'NSW Labor has zero tolerance of any behaviour which harms children.'

A couple of stories about the case were published during the final trial, but Munnings was only referred to by Central Coast media as a 'former pastor'.

Despite Munnings being outed as a paedophile, his company Crakyl Pty Ltd is still listed on The Lobbyists Register, granting him access to political decision-makers

That entry states Crakyl's employees - Munnings and his wife - are 'authorised to communicate and meet with NSW Government Officials for the purpose of lobbying' from August 2024.

Crakyl's clients include another family business, Munnings and Associates, Australian Chinese Consultancy Service, and south coast property development company Sealark.

Munnings flew to China in April last year for a trip which included attending a business conference in Guangzhou as a representative of the Australian Guangdong Chamber of Commerce (AGCC).

He was even interviewed by local reporters after viewing a demonstration of Chinese robots and commented on Australia's relations with international trading partners.

Munnings had repeatedly been set to stand trial as early as 2020, only for proceedings to be continually pushed back or aborted. He is now in Parklea prison (above)

Munnings was the AGCC's government relations adviser and had been described by the chamber as playing 'a vital role in supporting China–Australia trade and investment initiatives'.

Until Monday, his photograph and biography featured on the AGCC's website, but after being contacted by Daily Mail the chamber completely distanced itself from him.

'Mr Munnings does not hold any current position or advisory role with AGCC and has no authority to act or speak on the Chamber's behalf,' a spokesperson said.

'The website has now been updated, and Mr Munnings is no longer listed as holding any role with AGCC.'

Following his arrest, Munnings had been granted bail by police on conditions including that he surrender his passport and not approach any international points of departure.

He was able to travel to China after successfully seeking a bail variation in February last year whereby his expired passport was returned so he could obtain a new one.

He was permitted to leave Australia between April 14 and April 29, 2025, after providing an itinerary with proof of a return airfare within that date range to the DPP and police.

Munnings technically remains an Anglican priest until the Diocese of Newcastle is provided with a certificate of conviction, which will allow his removal from holy orders.
